# Independent audit of sparse-slack reconstruction and the global quadrilateral reduction

Source read in full: `candidate 9e9a3ee2a80ec95a`.

**Result: PASS, no repair needed.** This audit checks the complete dependency chain through the independently audited fixed-sector row-maximizer theorem and the exact reciprocal/PSD realization theorem. It does not assert the remaining quadrilateral row inequality or any mixed-fiber reconstruction.

## 1. Forced inverse columns and singular components

For a connected PD Z-matrix, the strictly convex coercive energy has its unique minimizer C^{-1}e_j. Passing to coordinatewise absolute values decreases neither the linear reward nor increases the quadratic cost, so uniqueness makes the minimizer nonnegative. A zero coordinate cannot be j, since its row would have nonpositive left side and positive right side. At any other zero coordinate, all negative-edge neighbors must also be zero. Connectivity propagates this to j, a contradiction. Thus every coordinate is strictly positive, including the singleton case.

For a connected singular PSD Z-matrix, absolute values of a least Rayleigh vector give a nonnegative kernel vector, and zero propagation makes it positive. Conjugation by its positive diagonal gives a weighted graph Laplacian: all row sums vanish, the off-diagonal edge weights are negative, and its quadratic form is the sum of positive edge weights times squared coordinate differences. Connectedness gives exactly a one-dimensional kernel. This verifies the rank count, not just existence of one null vector.

## 2. Exact reciprocal construction and turn formula

The concatenated vector w is positive and satisfies Lw>=0, with one nonzero forcing coordinate per PD component and none on singular components. The harmonic edge charges are the same formulas as in the audited direct PSD construction; those formulas require only Lw>=0 and never require w to be an eigenvector. Their harmonic value is h_i and their node slack is exactly delta_i=(Lw)_i/w_i.

The proposed u_i,v_i are finite, strictly positive, sum to t_i, and recover those harmonic charges. On a core edge, midpoint insertion has zero charge and introduces no geometry choice. Thus the exact finite convexity theorem supplies an actual convex polygon with the prescribed endpoints and all sector areas, including every zero-excess boundary case.

The inserted turn is exactly (t_i-1)D_i. The prescribed-endpoint turn is exactly

    u_(i-1)v_i D_(i-1)D_i delta_i.

To check the latter identity directly, divide the determinant by u_(i-1)v_i; the remaining expression is kappa_i-D_i a_(i-1)/u_(i-1)-D_(i-1)a_i/v_i, which is D_(i-1)D_i times the node budget slack. Its prefactor is positive even when a neighboring edge is a core. Therefore precisely the p positive-excess inserted points and the one selected ray point in each PD block are strict vertices. All other points are straight joins of the actual convex boundary; positivity of the radial data and interior source exclude reversals or a collapsed body.

## 3. Rank and the essential core hypothesis

With at least one core edge, the positive-edge graph is a forest of paths and singletons. It has m-p components. If s are singular and d_0 are PD, then p+d_0=m-s. Each singular component has nullity one and each PD component nullity zero, so rank L=m-s as well. Thus this particular reconstruction has exactly rank L vertices.

The full-positive-cycle case is explicitly excluded, correctly: there p=m but the graph has one component, so the forest identity would be false. No rank-controlled vertex assertion is made there. The construction handles multiple core edges, adjacent cores, PD singletons, and singular singletons without changing any prescribed data.

## 4. Application to row maxima

The previously audited fixed-sector extremum theorem supplies actual attainment, at least two core sectors, and at least two singular components at every selected-row maximum. Its arguments do not use a cap ceiling or profile condition. Therefore the forest reconstruction applies with m=6 and yields rank L=6-s<=4. Actual full-dimensional realization guarantees at least three vertices, giving a triangle or quadrilateral.

The first optimization keeps the six original sector areas fixed while possibly changing the six radii to maximize the selected row. The second, sparse-slack reconstruction keeps BOTH those maximizing radii and the same sector areas fixed, so it preserves the maximizing row exactly. Total area, cap areas, and all cap-profile conditions are unchanged. The ordinary invertible normalization changes all areas by one common factor and preserves the corresponding row normalization; it makes no lattice-preservation claim.

The conclusion is therefore a valid global ordinary reduction, one selected row at a time, with no cap-fraction restriction. Different rows may require different maximizing polygons, as stated. No neighbor-fiber compatibility, common mixed center, or general Lorentz inequality is inferred.

## 5. Relation to previous counts

The earlier least-eigenvector realization correctly made every node of a PD block a vertex. Its larger counts were sufficient upper bounds, not invariants of the prescribed data. Concentrating the forcing at one node makes every other node slack zero and preserves the same harmonic feasibility system, so the new smaller count does not contradict those earlier actual polygons. It supersedes the pentagon/hexagon reconstruction bounds without requiring their case-specific cap exclusions.
